claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by chemical-disorder-induced electron scattering.
Chemical disorder suppresses the superconducting transition temperature of HEAs relative to structurally similar low-entropy alloys.
Random atomic site occupation increases electron scattering.
Increased electron scattering reduces the electron mean free path.
A reduced electron mean free path weakens Cooper pairing.
Increasing the number and changing the type of principal elements while holding crystal structure and average electron count constant increases configurational entropy and chemical disorder.
The degree of chemical disorder can be quantified using configurational entropy or site-occupancy randomness.
Greater chemical disorder enhances electron scattering.
HEAs with greater chemical disorder will have lower transition temperatures than low-entropy alloys with similar structures and electron counts.
HEAs with greater chemical disorder will have smaller superconducting volume fractions than comparable low-entropy alloys.
Transition temperature will decrease monotonically as configurational entropy increases.
Annealing the samples minimizes extrinsic defects.
The proposed relationship applies when crystal structure and average electron count are controlled and chemical disorder is the varying factor.
The proposed relationship is not expected to apply when magnetic impurities dominate superconducting behavior.
The proposed relationship is not expected to apply when crystal structure changes with composition.
Electron mean free path can be inferred from resistivity measurements.
The magnitude of transition-temperature suppression may depend on the specific elements used.
